content: Down syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21, either in whole or in part. This condition is associated with varying degrees of intellectual disability, characteristic physical growth delays, and distinct facial features. It can be diagnosed prenatally or at birth. The condition was first described in 1866 by Dr. John Langdon Down, a British physician. In 1959, Dr. Jérôme Lejeune identified the underlying cause of Down syndrome as trisomy 21, the presence of an extra 21st chromosome. Dr. Down initially categorized individuals with this condition based on anthropometric measurements and facial features, though his terminology and classification have since been replaced with more ethical and accurate descriptors. Down syndrome is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability. The additional copy of chromosome 21 leads to overexpression of genes located on this chromosome, resulting in a wide range of clinical manifestations. The mechanisms leading to trisomy 21 include meiotic nondisjunction during meiosis I (most common), meiosis II errors, Robertsonian translocation, and mosaicism (rare). Advanced maternal age is a significant risk factor, as it contributes to cellular protein degradation affecting spindle formation, chromatid cohesion, and chromatid separation during oocyte division. Reduced maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and unconjugated estriol (uE3), along with elevated human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels, are often observed in pregnancies affected by Down syndrome. Prenatal diagnosis of Down syndrome is suggested by findings such as increased nuchal translucency on ultrasound, decreased levels of pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A), and abnormal quad screen results (elevated beta-hCG and inhibin A, decreased AFP and estriol). Differential diagnoses for low AFP levels include Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) and Patau syndrome (trisomy 13). In newborns, Down syndrome should be differentiated from other congenital conditions presenting with hypotonia, poor feeding, growth delays, and dysmorphic features, such as congenital hypothyroidism, isolated hypotonia, and Zellweger syndrome. Epidemiologically, Down syndrome occurs across all racial and socioeconomic groups. Approximately 3,000 to 5,000 children are born with this condition annually in the United States, with an estimated 250,000 families affected. While the risk of having a child with Down syndrome increases with maternal age, 80% of affected children are born to mothers younger than 35 years. Common risk factors for Down syndrome include maternal smoking, advanced maternal age, impaired recombination of chromosome 21, folate metabolism defects, and oral contraceptive use. Less common risk factors include maternal genomic instability, radiation exposure, low socioeconomic status, and maternal obesity. At birth, 50% of infants with Down syndrome have one or more serious congenital abnormalities, such as congenital heart defects (e.g., atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus). Other complications include hearing loss, diabetes, celiac disease, cataracts, endocarditis, atlantoaxial subluxation, thyroid dysfunction, duodenal atresia, and Hirschsprung disease. Life expectancy is approximately 50–55 years. Intellectual disability is universal, with a mean IQ of 42 by age 21. Alzheimer’s disease develops in 11% of individuals by age 50 and in 77% by age 70, with a mean onset age of 56 years. Diagnosis of Down syndrome is confirmed through cytogenetic studies demonstrating trisomy 21. Additional laboratory evaluations include complete blood counts to rule out leukemia and thyroid function tests (TSH and T4) at birth, 6 months, 1 year, and annually thereafter to monitor for hypothyroidism. Low levels of IgG subclass 4 are associated with increased susceptibility to bacterial infections. Mosaic trisomy 21 can be identified through lymphocyte preparations, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and buccal mucosa cell analysis. Imaging studies, such as X-rays, may reveal complications like congenital heart defects, atlantoaxial subluxation, or skeletal abnormalities. Ultrasound findings in affected fetuses may include increased nuchal fold thickness, duodenal atresia (double-bubble sign), shortened humerus and femur, and other markers. Echocardiography is essential for evaluating congenital heart defects, which are present in 40–60% of individuals with Down syndrome. Treatment is tailored to the specific manifestations of the condition. For example, congenital heart defects may require corrective surgery shortly after birth. Regular follow-up is critical to monitor growth, hearing, vision, thyroid function, cardiac health, and hematological status. Preventive care includes genetic counseling for families with a history of Down syndrome and prenatal screening for at-risk pregnancies. Comprehensive care also involves routine vaccinations and adherence to standard newborn, childhood, and adult screening programs.
